t: Ibn Sina set out the medical knowledge of his time in five ordered books, fitting the traditions of Galen and Hippocrates into Aristotle's natural philosophy.
Its Latin translation entered European scholastic medicine, and university courses used the text from the 14th century onwards.
It lost ground in the 16th century as humanists preferred Greek and Roman authorities to Arabic ones, but it was still taught as background literature in Padua in 1715.
dyk: The Canon gives seven rules for experimenting with new drugs, taken partly from Galen, among them that a drug should be tested on a single condition rather than a composite one and that experiments should be carried out on the human body.
ev: Ibn Sina completes the Canon in Hamadan
The date of the earliest known copy of volume 5, now in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto
The Canon is translated from Arabic into Latin in Toledo
Nathan ha-Meati translates the Canon into Hebrew, and medical scholars in Europe begin to use it
The earliest printed edition of the Latin Canon appears, covering only book three
Latin editions, fourteen of them in the 16th century, continue until this year
The Canon is still taught as background literature at Padua

f.made: Ibn Sina (Avicenna), who began it in Gorganj, continued it in Rey and completed it in Hamadan in 1025, drawing on Greco-Roman, Persian, Chinese and Indian medicine
f.form: An Arabic encyclopedia of medicine in five books: principles and anatomy, a materia medica of about 800 simple substances, diseases by body part, diseases of more than one part, and a formulary of 650 compound drugs
f.where: Read in Arabic and in Latin, Hebrew, Turkish and Persian translations; the earliest known copy of volume 5, dated 1052, is in the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto
f.known: the five-book plan; the materia medica; seven rules for testing new drugs; descriptions of stroke and of the nervous system; the long treatment of fevers; its place as the standard medical textbook of European universities
